newsitem.title: MONACO: SOCCER-WORKAHOLIC TIGANA TRIUMPHS IN IDLE PRINCIPALITY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WORKAHOLIC TIGANA TRIUMPHS IN IDLE PRINCIPALITY.

text.p: Jean Tigana, the man who brought Monaco their sixth French soccer league title on the 700th anniversary of the Grimaldi dynasty, has little of the glamour usually associated with the Mediterranean principality.

The former international midfielder, who came to Monaco in the middle of the 1995-96 season after the controversial departure of Arsene Wenger, does not belong to the idle jet set. Instead, he believes in the virtues of hard work and effort.

"It's hard work I expect from players and it's hard work I expect from myself. I don't know if the players feel it but I try to adapt my actions to my words," he said after Monaco celebrated their first title since 1988 on Sunday.
Actually, Tigana has not changed much since he lined up alongside Michel Platini in the French team which won the 1984 European championships. He has always been an austere, disciplined character.
"I was the same as a player. I tried to lead a healthy life and I feel I can ask the same of my players now," he said.
"People say Monaco play beautiful football but we achieve this through discipline. Only discipline allows invention and creativity to develop."

Tigana added he had made this attitude a way of life. It is one which enabled him to rise from a poor childhood in a working class suburb of Marseille to a triumph in one of the wealthiest places on earth, at the age of 41.
"Discipline is what keeps me going. My progress in life has been extraordinary when you think about where I come from and where I am now. I have the impression I'm living in a daydream," he said.

That is why one should not expect the Malian-born Tigana, who owns a renowned vineyard in Medoc but does not drink, to show any excessive joy after this long-awaited title. He has already set his sights on the future.
"Next season will be very important. We must realise that it is going to be more diificult to get back to work. Discipline is difficult to accept," he said.
"We saw what happened to Nantes and Auxerre, they crashed the year after winning the title".

Tigana had something to prove after failing to change the team's attitude when he joined in mid-season last year. The year before, he led Lyon to second place in the league and narrowly missed the top spot.
"I knew from the start that we (Monaco) had what it took to win the league," he said.
"The first year, we were not on the same wave length because they (the players) had had four different coaches in the same season. I had problems to solve because we did not speak the same language".
This season, in contrast, the players fully understood Tigana's message. Work hard.
Behind his no-nonsense approach also lies an enormous ambition.
"I want to equal as a coach my record of five league titles as a player," said Tigana, who won his championship medals with Bordeaux and Marseille.
"But to achieve this I don't want to end up coaching at the age of 75 like (former Anderlecht and Marseille coach) Raymond Goethals," he added.
Another thing Tigana wishes to achieve is to reach the final of a European cup competition.

In 1991, Goethals left him out of the European Cup final between Marseille and Red Star Belgrade and this year, after a disastrous first leg in Milan (3-1), Monaco bowed out of the UEFA Cup in the semifinals against Internazionale.
These remain two of Tigana's bitterest memories but his latest triumph will give him the chance to rectify that in the European Cup next year.
